newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian scientist defends malaria vaccine.
newsitem.headline: Colombian scientist defends malaria vaccine.

text.p: Colombian scientist Manuel Elkin Patarroyo rejected U.S. and British criticisms on Monday about the effectiveness of the anti-malaria vaccine he invented.

He blamed errors in the way the drug had been manufactured in the United States for recent test failures and said strong commercial interests were at work to discredit the Spf 66 vaccine, which, if proved to work, could protect 2.5 billion people at risk throughout the Tropics.

"These criticisms have been an extremely harsh blow. They say the vaccine doesn't work but I don't accept that. What doesn't work is the vaccine they produced in the United States," Patarroyo said in an interview with Colombia's Caracol radio network.

The researcher claimed that batches of the synthetic vaccine produced in Colombia and distributed nationally as well as to Venezuela, Ecuador and Tanzania had proved effective in 31 percent to 55 percent of those treated.
He told Caracol that each stage of the chemical production process had to be supervised carefully otherwise faults could occur.
In 1990 Patarroyo handed over the manufacturing rights of the vaccine to the World Health Organisation and also gave the go-head to the U.S. army to produce it.
The U.S. head of malaria research had called the effectiveness of Spf 66 into question.

In a recent article, the British medical journal The Lancet also cast doubt on how useful the vaccine really was in controlling the disease, which causes fever and has developed strains, some of which can be fatal and are increasingly resistant to traditional prophylactic drugs.

Patarroyo said in his interview with Caracol that he was looking to set up a plant to produce the vaccine in Colombia and said he would soon publish fresh results about its effectiveness, backed by the World Health Organisation and other international medical bodies.
